The defendant must perform an act which is 'more than merely preparatory' to the commission of the offence

bank.question: What is the minimum percentage of votes required to pass a 'special resolution' at a general meeting of a private limited company?
bank.explanation: A 'special resolution' requires a majority of not less than 75% of the votes cast by shareholders.
options: A simple majority (more than 50%)
A two-thirds majority (66.6%)
A majority of not less than 75%
Unanimous consent of all shareholders

bank.question: When does an express legal easement created by deed over registered land become effective at law?
bank.explanation: Section 27 of the Land Registration Act 2002 requires an express grant of an easement for a term of years absolute to be completed by registration to operate at law.
options: At the time the deed is signed and witnessed
When the easement is entered on the register of the servient land
When the dominant owner first uses the right of way
As soon as the parties agree the terms in writing

bank.question: Which of the following serves as a partial defence to murder, resulting in a conviction for voluntary manslaughter?
bank.explanation: Loss of control (Coronado/Section 54 Coroners and Justice Act 2009) is a partial defence that reduces a charge of murder to voluntary manslaughter.
options: Loss of control
Self-defence
Duress
Automatism

bank.question: Under the Theft Act 1968, in which of the following circumstances can a person be guilty of stealing land?
bank.explanation: Under s 4(1) of the Theft Act 1968, land cannot generally be stolen unless the person is a trustee or representative, or if they sever and take things forming part of the land.
options: The person honestly believes they have a legal right to the land
The person is a trustee or personal representative and deals with the land in breach of confidence
The person is a squatter who has occupied the land for more than 10 years
The person destroys a boundary fence to increase the size of their own garden

bank.question: A claimant has an unusually thin skull and suffers a severe brain injury from a minor blow caused by the defendant's negligence. Which principle ensures the defendant is liable for the full extent of the harm?
bank.explanation: The 'but for' test establishes factual causation; the 'thin skull' rule (talem qualem) ensures the defendant is liable for the full extent of injuries due to a physical vulnerability.
options: Novus actus interveniens
Res ipsa loquitur
The thin skull rule
The 'but for' test

bank.question: In the absence of a written partnership agreement, which of the following events will automatically cause the dissolution of a partnership under the Partnership Act 1890?
bank.explanation: Under the Partnership Act 1890, unless there is an agreement to the contrary, a partnership is dissolved by the death or bankruptcy of any partner.
options: The death of any partner
The partner with the largest capital contribution reaches retirement age
A partner is diagnosed with a temporary illness
The firm changes its primary business address

bank.question: A claimant applies for an interim payment in a personal injury case. Which of the following conditions must be met for the court to make such an order under the Civil Procedure Rules?
bank.explanation: Interim payments under CPR 25.7 require the defendant to have admitted liability or for the court to be satisfied the claimant would obtain judgment for a substantial sum.
options: The claimant is in urgent need of funds to pay for medical treatment
The claimant has requested the payment in the claim form
The defendant is a local authority with substantial assets
The defendant has admitted liability in full for the claimant's damages

bank.question: A company assigns its right to receive a debt to a third party. What is the effect of the 'subject to equities' rule in this context?
bank.explanation: The common law rule (supported by s 136 Law of Property Act 1925) is that an assignee cannot be in a better position than the assignor and takes the debt subject to any existing equities.
options: The debtor can no longer rely on any defences they had against the assignor
The assignee takes the assignment subject to any equities (defences) the debtor had against the assignor
The assignee is entitled to claim more than the sum originally owed to the assignor
The assignment must be made orally to be legally binding

bank.question: What is the standard of care required of a director under s 174 of the Companies Act 2006 (Duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence)?
bank.explanation: Under s 174 of the Companies Act 2006, a director must exercise the care, skill, and diligence that would be exercised by a reasonably diligent person with both the general knowledge/skill expected of the role and the actual knowledge/skill they possess.
options: A purely subjective test based on the director's actual experience
A purely objective test based on a reasonable person
A dual objective and subjective test
A test based solely on the specific requirements of the company's Articles

bank.question: Which of the following rights under the European Convention on Human Rights is classified as a 'qualified' right?
bank.explanation: The Article 8 right to respect for private and family life is a qualified right, meaning it can be interfered with if the interference is in accordance with the law and necessary in a democratic society.
options: The right to respect for private and family life (Article 8)
The prohibition of torture (Article 3)
The prohibition of slavery and forced labour (Article 4)
The right to a fair trial (Article 6)

bank.question: In the context of registered land, what is meant by the 'mirror principle'?
bank.explanation: The 'mirror principle' aims to ensure that the land register reflects all relevant interests in the land, so a buyer can rely on it.
options: The principle that a buyer's interest must reflect the seller's exactly
The principle that land must be registered in the names of all occupiers
The principle that the register should be a complete and accurate reflection of the state of the title
The principle that all land transfers must be made by deed

bank.question: A solicitor wants to act for two different clients in the same matter where there is a conflict of interest. According to the SRA Code of Conduct, in which limited circumstance might this be permitted?
bank.explanation: Under the SRA Code of Conduct, a solicitor may only act where there is a conflict of interest if the clients have a substantially common interest and have given informed consent in writing.
options: The solicitor believes they can act fairly for both
The clients have both verbally agreed to the representation
The clients have a substantially common interest and have given informed consent in writing
The solicitor is at a firm with more than 50 partners

bank.question: To be convicted of basic criminal damage, which of the following mental states must the prosecution prove?
bank.explanation: The mens rea for criminal damage (s 1 Criminal Damage Act 1971) is intention or recklessness as to the destruction or damage of property belonging to another.
options: The defendant was negligent as to whether the property would be damaged
The defendant was reckless as to whether the property would be damaged
The defendant intended to trespass on the property
The defendant failed to take reasonable care to protect the property

bank.question: Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, which type of bill can become law without the consent of the House of Lords after a delay of only one month?
bank.explanation: The House of Commons has the 'financial privilege' to pass a 'money bill' without the consent of the House of Lords after a one-month delay under the Parliament Act 1911.
options: A 'money bill' dealing only with taxation or public spending
A bill to extend the maximum duration of Parliament
A bill introduced in the House of Lords
A bill to reform the judiciary

bank.question: Which of the following best describes an 'invitation to treat' in the law of contract?
bank.explanation: In contract law, an 'invitation to treat' is an indication of willingness to receive offers, such as a display of goods in a shop window.
options: A binding offer that can be accepted
A counter-offer that rejects the original offer
An invitation to others to make an offer
A contract that is voidable due to duress

bank.question: In a claim for defamation under the Defamation Act 2013, what must a claimant prove regarding the impact of the statement on their reputation?
bank.explanation: Under Section 1 of the Defamation Act 2013, a statement is not defamatory unless its publication has caused or is likely to cause serious harm to the reputation of the claimant.
options: The statement was published to at least one third party
The publication has caused or is likely to cause serious harm to the reputation of the claimant
The statement is proven to be factually false in every detail
The defendant acted with malice or an intent to injure the claimant's reputation

bank.question: A solicitor receives a cheque for pounds10,000 from a client to be used for the payment of stamp duty. Where must the solicitor deposit this money?
bank.explanation: Under the Solicitors' Accounts Rules, money held on behalf of a client must be paid into a client account without delay, unless an exception applies.
options: Into the firm's office account, provided it is moved within 48 hours
Into the solicitor's personal savings account for safekeeping
Into a client account
Into a suspense account until the completion of the matter

bank.question: What is the 'actus reus' of the offence of conspiracy under the Criminal Law Act 1977?
bank.explanation: Under s.1(1) of the Criminal Law Act 1977, the actus reus of conspiracy is an agreement between two or more people to carry out a criminal course of conduct.
options: An agreement between two or more people to carry out a criminal course of conduct
Taking a substantial step towards the commission of a crime
Assisting or encouraging another person to commit an offence
Committing an act which is more than merely preparatory to the commission of an offence

bank.question: A buyer enters into a contract to purchase a registered freehold property, but the completion is set for six months later. How should the buyer protect their interest in the meantime?
bank.explanation: Equitable interests in land, such as an estate contract, must be protected by a notice on the charges register of the affected title to bind a purchaser for value.
options: By filing a caution against first registration
By entering a restriction in the proprietorship register
By physical possession of the property
By entering a notice on the charges register of the seller's title

bank.question: An employer is planning to make 120 employees redundant at a single establishment within a 90-day period. What is the minimum period for collective consultation before the first dismissal takes effect?
bank.explanation: Section 188 of the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992 requires consultation to begin at least 45 days in advance if 100 or more redundancies are proposed.
options: 30 days
14 days
45 days
90 days

bank.question: A buyer and seller agree orally to the sale of a piece of land. Why is this agreement generally unenforceable in a court of law?
bank.explanation: The doctrine of part performance was largely abolished by the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, which requires contracts for the sale of land to be in writing.
options: Privity of contract
Section 2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989
The rule in Rylands v Fletcher
The doctrine of laches

bank.question: Under the Companies (Model Articles) Regulations 2008 for a private company limited by shares, what is the default quorum for a meeting of the directors?
bank.explanation: Under the Model Articles, a quorum for a meeting of the directors is typically two, unless otherwise specified.
options: Two
A simple majority of all directors
Three
One

bank.question: In a negligence claim, the court determines that the damage suffered by the claimant was not a reasonably foreseeable consequence of the defendant's breach. Which legal principle does this relate to?
bank.explanation: The 'But For' test is used for factual causation, but the 'Remoteness' test (Wagon Mound No 1) determines if the type of damage was reasonably foreseeable.
options: Factual causation
Contributory negligence
Remoteness of damage
Res ipsa loquitur

bank.question: Under the Human Rights Act 1998, what is the standard limitation period for bringing a claim against a public authority for a breach of a Convention right?
bank.explanation: Human rights claims against public authorities for breaches of the ECHR under the Human Rights Act 1998 must generally be brought within one year.
options: Three years
Six years
One year
Six months

bank.question: A husband and wife own a house as joint tenants. The husband asks the wife to sign a charge over the house to secure a loan for his business. What is the bank's duty to avoid 'undue influence' claims?
bank.explanation: The 'O'Brien' guidelines suggest that if a surety is in a non-commercial relationship with the debtor, the lender is put on inquiry to ensure the surety understands the risks.
options: The bank must provide independent legal advice to the wife itself
The bank is put on inquiry and must take reasonable steps to ensure the wife understands the risks
The charge is automatically void if the wife does not benefit from the loan
The bank must ensure the wife pays for her own valuation of the property

bank.question: Which of the following describes the five elements of the 'actus reus' and 'mens rea' of theft?
bank.explanation: Under s.1(1) of the Theft Act 1968, the five elements are: appropriation, property, belonging to another, dishonesty, and intention to permanently deprive.
options: Appropriation, property, belonging to another, dishonesty, intention to permanently deprive
Touching, property, belonging to another, recklessness, intention to keep
Asportation, ownership, belonging to another, dishonesty, intention to borrow
Conversion, property, belonging to another, negligence, intention to permanently deprive

bank.question: In civil litigation, which of the following is a formal mechanism used by parties to settle a dispute before trial with specific cost consequences if the offer is not beaten?
bank.explanation: A Part 36 offer is a formal offer to settle. If the claimant rejects it and fails to beat it at trial, they usually face cost penalties.
options: An application for summary judgment
A request for further information under Part 18
A witness statement of fact
A Part 36 offer

bank.question: Which of the following describes the principle established in Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897]?
bank.explanation: A limited company is a separate legal person from its shareholders and directors. This 'veil' protects individuals from personal liability for the company's debts.
options: The directors are always personally liable for the company's debts
The company has a separate legal personality distinct from its members
Shareholders have unlimited liability for the company's debts
The company cannot own property in its own name

bank.question: In the context of registered land, which of the following interests will typically be an 'overriding interest' under Schedule 3 of the Land Registration Act 2002?
bank.explanation: Equitable interests in registered land that are not protected by a notice on the register can be overridden if the person is in actual occupation, unless they failed to disclose the interest upon inquiry.
options: A person in actual occupation of the land
A person with an unrecorded legal easement
A person with a restrictive covenant not noted on the charges register
A beneficiary under a trust of land who is not in occupation

bank.question: A solicitor receives pounds5,000 from a client to be held on account of future disbursements in a conveyancing transaction. According to the SRA Accounts Rules, where should this money be paid?
bank.explanation: Client money must be paid into a client account without delay. A cheque for costs already billed is generally considered office money, but a refund for the client must go to the client account.
options: The solicitor's personal bank account
The firm's business (office) account
A client account
A suspense account

bank.question: Under the law of contract, what is the effect of an offeree making a counter-offer?
bank.explanation: A counter-offer operates as a rejection of the original offer. Once rejected, the original offer is terminated and cannot be accepted later unless it is renewed.
options: The offeree has accepted the original offer with conditions
The original offer remains open for acceptance for 24 hours
The offeror must accept the counter-offer
The original offer is terminated and cannot be later accepted

bank.question: Under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, when can a third party enforce a term of a contract?
bank.explanation: A non-party may enforce a contract term if the contract expressly provides for it or the term purports to confer a benefit on them, unless the parties did not intend it to be enforceable.
options: Only if the third party has provided consideration
If the contract term purports to confer a benefit on the third party and the parties intended it to be enforceable
Only if the third party was present when the contract was signed
If the third party is a close relative of the promisee

bank.question: Which article of the European Convention on Human Rights is an 'absolute' right that can never be restricted by the state?
bank.explanation: An Absolute Right (like Article 3) cannot be balanced against the public interest or restricted under any circumstances, unlike Qualified or Limited rights.
options: Article 3 (Prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment)
Article 8 (Right to respect for private and family life)
Article 10 (Freedom of expression)
Article 11 (Freedom of assembly and association)

bank.question: What is the primary duty of a director under section 172 of the Companies Act 2006?
bank.explanation: Section 172 requires a director to act in the way they consider, in good faith, would be most likely to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole.
options: To exercise reasonable care, skill, and diligence
To act in accordance with the company's constitution
To promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole
To avoid conflicts of interest

bank.question: To be guilty of burglary under s 9(1)(a) of the Theft Act 1968, a person must enter a building as a trespasser with intent to do what?
bank.explanation: Burglary under section 9(1)(a) requires the intent to commit one of three specified offences (theft, GBH, or unlawful damage) at the time of entry. Possession of stolen goods isn't one of them.
options: Inflict grievous bodily harm on any person therein
Steal anything in the building or part of the building
Do unlawful damage to the building or anything therein
Be in possession of stolen goods

bank.question: Which statement best describes the principle of Parliamentary Sovereignty in the UK?
bank.explanation: Parliamentary Sovereignty means Parliament is the supreme legal authority and no court can strike down an Act of Parliament. No Parliament can bind its successors.
options: The courts have the power to strike down primary legislation
Parliament cannot pass a law that a future Parliament cannot repeal
The House of Lords is more powerful than the House of Commons
Acts of Parliament can only be changed by the Monarch

bank.question: In the law of tort, the 'but for' test is used to establish which of the following?
bank.explanation: The 'but for' test determines factual causation: but for the defendant's breach of duty, would the claimant have suffered the loss? If yes, the defendant is not liable.
options: Factual causation
Remoteness of damage
Contributory negligence
Professional negligence

bank.question: If a defendant in a civil claim wishes to defend the entire claim after being served with a claim form and particulars, what is the standard time limit?
bank.explanation: Acknowledge the claim within 14 days, then serve a defence within 28 days of the claim form. Filing an Acknowledgement extends the initial 14-day defence deadline.
options: File a defence within 7 days
File an acknowledgement of service within 28 days
File an acknowledgement of service within 14 days and a defence within 28 days of service of the particulars
Wait for the court to set a trial date

bank.question: Under the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, when is a solicitor permitted to act for two clients in a matter where there is a conflict of interest?
bank.explanation: Solicitors cannot act for two or more clients if there is a conflict of interest or a significant risk of one, unless one of the limited exceptions (e.g. substantially common interest) applies.
options: If both clients are members of the same family
If there is a 'substantially common interest' between the clients and the requirements of the exception are met
Whenever both clients give verbal consent to the solicitor
If the solicitor is the only legal professional in the local area

bank.question: Under the SRA Principles, which of the following is a mandatory requirement for all solicitors?
bank.explanation: Under the SRA Principles 2019, acting with integrity is a fundamental requirement and is considered a core professional duty that underpins all legal work.
options: To act in the best interests of the firm
To act with integrity
To ensure the firm remains profitable
To provide the cheapest possible service to clients

bank.question: Which of the following best describes the formal requirements for a contract for the sale of land?
bank.explanation: Under s 2 Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, a contract for the sale of land must be in writing, incorporate all agreed terms, and be signed by both parties.
options: A contract for the sale of land must be in writing and signed by both parties
Every contract for the sale of land must be made by deed
Oral contracts for land are valid if there are witnesses present
Only the seller needs to sign the contract for it to be enforceable

bank.question: In a personal injury claim, if a defendant's negligence triggers a pre-existing condition in the claimant, what principle applies?
bank.explanation: The 'eggshell skull' rule means a defendant must take their victim as they find them, even if the victim's physical condition makes the injury worse.
options: The claimant was contributorily negligent
The harm was too remote to be foreseeable
The defendant must take the victim as they find them
The defendant is not liable for secondary victims

bank.question: An employer refuses to promote an employee solely because they believe the employee is 'too old' for the new role. What type of discrimination is this?
bank.explanation: Direct discrimination occurs when someone is treated less favourably because of a protected characteristic like age, as per the Equality Act 2010.
options: Indirect discrimination
Direct discrimination
Harassment
Victimisation

bank.question: A solicitor is acting for a corporate client and is asked to hold funds in the firm's office account rather than the client account. What is the requirement?
bank.explanation: If a donor is not a retail client, the solicitor must explain that the funds will not have the same protections as client money under the SRA Accounts Rules.
options: The money must be returned to the client immediately
The money must be placed in a designated client account within 48 hours
The solicitor must inform the SRA of the transaction
The solicitor must explain that the money will not be protected by the SRA Accounts Rules

bank.question: Under the Companies Act 2006, what is the default percentage of votes required to pass an Ordinary Resolution?
bank.explanation: An Ordinary Resolution requires a simple majority (more than 50%) of the votes cast by shareholders present and voting.
options: A simple majority (more than 50%)
A 75% majority
Unanimous consent
A majority of two-thirds

bank.question: A person enters a shop as a trespasser and, once inside, steals a laptop. Which section of the Theft Act 1968 most accurately covers this?
bank.explanation: Burglary under s 9(1)(b) occurs when a person, having entered as a trespasser, steals or attempts to steal or inflicts or attempts to inflict GBH.
options: Theft Act 1968, s 8
Theft Act 1968, s 9(1)(a)
Theft Act 1968, s 9(1)(b)
Theft Act 1968, s 10

bank.question: The UK Constitution is often described as being built upon the separation of powers. Which three branches does this involve?
bank.explanation: Separation of powers involves the independent functioning of the Legislature (Parliament), Executive (Government), and the Judiciary (Courts).
options: The Queen, the Prime Minister, and the Lords
The Police, the Courts, and the Prisons
The Local Authorities, the Civil Service, and the Cabinet
The Legislature, the Executive, and the Judiciary

bank.question: What is a common consequence if a claimant refuses a defendant's Part 36 offer and fails to obtain a more advantageous judgment at trial?
bank.explanation: Under CPR Part 36, if a claimant rejects a defendant's offer and fails to beat it at trial, they are usually liable for the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period.
options: The defendant must pay all the claimant's costs regardless
The claimant may be ordered to pay the defendant's costs from the date the offer expired
The case is automatically dismissed
The defendant must pay the claimant's costs on the indemnity basis

bank.question: Under Section 2 of the Human Rights Act 1998, what duty does a UK court have regarding decisions of the European Court of Human Rights?
bank.explanation: Section 2 of the HRA 1998 requires UK courts to 'take into account' judgments of the European Court of Human Rights but does not make them strictly binding.
options: They must ignore them to preserve Parliamentary Sovereignty
They must follow them as binding legal precedents
They must take them into account when determining a question
They must refer the matter to the Supreme Court for approval

bank.question: Which of the following interests is most likely to be an overriding interest in registered land?
bank.explanation: The beneficial interest of a person in actual occupation is an overriding interest under Schedule 3, Para 2 of the Land Registration Act 2002.
options: The interest of a person in actual occupation
A restrictive covenant created in 2015
An equitable mortgage
An option to purchase the land

bank.question: For a defendant to successfully plead the common law defence of self-defence, what must they generally demonstrate?
bank.explanation: To rely on the defence of self-defence, the force used must be 'reasonable in the circumstances' as the defendant honestly believed them to be.
options: That the force used was slight and caused no injury
That the defendant was an expert in martial arts
That the defendant warned the victim first
That the force used was reasonable in the circumstances

bank.question: In the law of contract, when is an acceptance by post generally deemed to be effective?
bank.explanation: Under the Postal Rule, acceptance by post is effective at the moment the letter is posted, provided it was reasonable to use the post.
options: When the offeror receives the letter
When the offeror reads the letter
When the letter is posted by the offeree
When the letter arrives at the offeror's address

bank.question: What is the standard limitation period for a claimant to bring a claim for damages for personal injury?
bank.explanation: Section 11(1) of the Limitation Act 1980 provides a three-year limitation period for personal injury claims, starting from the date of the accident or date of knowledge.
options: Three years from the date of the accident
Six years from the date of the accident
One year from the date of the accident
Two years from the date of the accident

bank.question: In Judicial Review, what does the ground of 'irrationality' (Wednesbury unreasonableness) primarily concern?
bank.explanation: In judicial review, 'irrationality' (Wednesbury unreasonableness) applies to decisions so outrageous that no sensible person could have arrived at them.
options: The decision-maker did not have the legal power to make the choice
The decision was so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it
The decision-maker failed to follow a mandatory statutory procedure
The decision-maker was biased against the claimant

bank.question: Under the Companies Act 2006, what is the minimum percentage of votes required to pass a Special Resolution?
bank.explanation: A special resolution requires a majority of not less than 75% of the votes cast by members entitled to vote.
options: More than 50% of the votes cast
At least 66% of the votes cast
Exactly 100% of the votes cast
Not less than 75% of the votes cast

bank.question: Under the SRA Code of Conduct, when must a solicitor inform a client of their right to complain and the existence of the Legal Ombudsman?
bank.explanation: The SRA Code of Conduct requires a solicitor to inform a client in writing at the outset of the matter about their right to complain and the right to use the Legal Ombudsman.
options: Only if the client expresses dissatisfaction during the case
In writing at the outset of the matter and at the conclusion of the complaints process
Verbally during the first meeting or telephone call
Only if the solicitor is a sole practitioner

bank.question: What is the definition of a 'strict liability' offence in criminal law?
bank.explanation: Strict liability offences do not require proof of a 'mens rea' (guilty mind) for at least one element of the actus reus.
options: An offence where the prosecution does not need to prove mens rea for at least one element of the actus reus
An offence where the defendant has no possible defence available
An offence that carries a mandatory life sentence
An offence where the defendant is guilty even if they did not commit the actus reus

bank.question: A firm refuses to interview a candidate because they are a wheelchair user. What type of discrimination under the Equality Act 2010 is this most likely to be?
bank.explanation: Direct discrimination occurs when a person is treated less favourably because of a protected characteristic, such as disability.
options: Indirect discrimination
Harassment
Direct discrimination
Victimisation

bank.question: In civil litigation, what is the purpose of an 'interim payment'?
bank.explanation: Interim payments are governed by CPR 25.7 and are intended to provide the claimant with money before the final trial where liability is likely to be established.
options: An advance payment on account of any damages the defendant may be held liable to pay
A payment made to the court to settle the case immediately
A payment made by the claimant to the defendant to stop the proceedings
A payment of the solicitor's costs before the trial begins

bank.question: Under the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, what is the requirement for a valid execution of a deed by an individual?
bank.explanation: Section 1(3) of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989 requires a deed to be in writing, clear that it is a deed, signed by the maker in the presence of a witness, and delivered.
options: Signed by the maker and an executor
Signed by the maker and a solicitor
Signed by the maker and notarised by a public notary
Signed by the maker in the presence of a witness who also signs it

bank.question: Which of the following are the three essential elements of the tort of negligence?
bank.explanation: To establish negligence, the claimant must prove a duty of care, a breach of that duty, and that the breach caused reasonably foreseeable damage.
options: Duty of care, intent to harm, and proximity
Duty of care, breach of duty, and causation of damage
A contract, a breach of contract, and financial loss
Actionable per se, malice, and lack of consent

bank.question: What is the primary purpose of the 'Conflict of Interest' rule in the SRA Code of Conduct?
bank.explanation: Conflict of interest rules generally prohibit acting for two clients whose interests are in direct conflict, unless a specific exception in the SRA Code applies.
options: To ensure the solicitor makes the maximum profit from both clients
To ensure the court is not misled by the solicitor's actions
To ensure the solicitor's ability to act in the best interests of each client is not compromised
To protect the solicitor from being sued by the SRA

bank.question: In a criminal trial, what is the standard of proof required for the prosecution to secure a conviction?
bank.explanation: The burden of proof in a criminal trial is on the prosecution, and the standard is 'beyond reasonable doubt' (or 'so that you are sure').
options: Beyond reasonable doubt
On the balance of probabilities
A high degree of probability
Beyond all possible doubt

bank.question: A man makes a will leaving pounds10,000 to his friend. The friend acts as one of the two witnesses to the man's signature. What is the legal effect produced by the friend witnessing the will?
bank.explanation: Under the Wills Act 1837, if a person witnesses a will, any gift made to that witness or their spouse/civil partner in the will is void.
options: The witness must return the gift to the estate for redistribution among other beneficiaries
The entire will is rendered invalid due to the conflict of interest
The gift to the witness is void, but the rest of the will remains valid
The gift remains valid as long as there were at least two other independent witnesses

bank.question: In company law, what type of report does an auditor issue if they are satisfied that the financial statements give a true and fair view of the company's state of affairs?
bank.explanation: An 'unqualified' report is issued when the auditor is satisfied that the accounts provide a true and fair view of the company's financial position.
options: An unqualified audit report
A qualified audit report
An adverse audit report
A disclaimer of opinion

bank.question: A solicitor receives pounds500 from a client to cover future court fees. The money is placed in the client account. The solicitor then pays the pounds500 court fee using that money. How should this payment be recorded?
bank.explanation: If the client's money is used for the client's own purposes (like paying a court fee), the transaction is recorded as a debit on the Client Ledger Account.
options: Credit on the Office Ledger Account
Debit on the Office Ledger Account
Credit on the Client Ledger Account
Debit on the Client Ledger Account

bank.question: To create a valid legal mortgage over a freehold property, which of the following formalities must be satisfied?
bank.explanation: Under the Law of Property Act 1925, a legal mortgage over land must be created by deed to be valid at law.
options: A written contract signed by both parties
A deed
An oral agreement witnessed by two people
A statutory declaration

bank.question: During a civil claim, a judge grants a party an extension of time to file an appeal. To which body can the opposing party appeal against the decision to grant this extension?
bank.explanation: Section 18 of the Senior Courts Act 1981 provides that there is no right of appeal against an order allowing an extension of time for appealing.
options: The Court of Appeal
The Supreme Court
There is no right of appeal against such an order
The High Court (Family Division)

bank.question: Under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE), at what point must a police officer normally 'caution' a suspect?
bank.explanation: Under the PACE Codes of Practice, a 'caution' must be given to a person whom there are grounds to suspect of an offence before they are questioned.
options: When the person is first seen by a police officer
When there are grounds to suspect the person has committed an offence
Only after the person has been formally charged
Only when the person arrives at the police station

bank.question: Which of the following best describes the principle of 'Promissory Estoppel' in contract law?
bank.explanation: Promissory estoppel is a suspensory doctrine; it prevents a party from enforcing their strict legal rights for a period, but does not create a new cause of action.
options: It can be used to create new legal rights where no contract exists
It requires that the person making the promise receives consideration
It acts as a 'shield, not a sword', meaning it is a defence and not a cause of action
It applies even if the person receiving the promise has not relied upon it

bank.question: A man shouts at a woman from across a busy motorway, 'I am going to come over there and hit you tomorrow!' The woman is frightened. Which offence has the man most likely committed?
bank.explanation: Assault requires the defendant to cause the victim to apprehend immediate unlawful personal violence; a threat of future violence does not meet the 'immediacy' requirement.
options: Battery
No offence, because the threat was not of 'immediate' violence
Assault
Affray

bank.question: In civil proceedings, how many days does a defendant usually have to file an acknowledgement of service after being served with a claim form within the jurisdiction?
bank.explanation: The 14-day period to file an acknowledgement of service or a defence starts from the date the claim form is served.
options: 14 days
7 days
21 days
28 days

bank.question: What happens if a settlor creates a valid discretionary trust but the sole trustee dies before the trust is administered?
bank.explanation: Equity will not allow a trust to fail for want of a trustee; the court or the settlor's personal representatives can appoint new ones.
options: The trust property reverts to the settlor's estate absolutely
The trust property goes to the Crown as bona vacantia
The trust is void for uncertainty
The court will appoint a new trustee to ensure the trust does not fail

bank.question: What is meant by a 'leapfrog' appeal in the English legal system?
bank.explanation: A 'leapfrog' appeal allows a case to go directly from the High Court to the Supreme Court, bypassing the Court of Appeal, usually for points of law of general public importance.
options: High Court to the Supreme Court
County Court to the Court of Appeal
Magistrates' Court to the Crown Court
Court of Appeal to the Privy Council

bank.question: An employer introduces a policy that all staff must work on Saturdays. This particularly affects employees of a certain religion who observe Saturday as a Sabbath. What type of discrimination is this?
bank.explanation: Indirect discrimination occurs when a policy (PCP) applies to everyone but puts a specific protected group at a disadvantage and cannot be objectively justified.
options: Direct discrimination
Harassment
Indirect discrimination
Victimisation

bank.question: A seller sends a quotation to a buyer on their standard terms. The buyer responds with a purchase order containing different terms. The seller then delivers the goods without further comment. Which terms apply?
bank.explanation: Standard terms of business constitute an offer. Since the buyer's purchase order contained different terms, it was a counter-offer which the seller accepted by performance (delivery).
options: The seller's terms apply because they were sent first
Neither party's terms apply; the contract is governed by the Sale of Goods Act 1979
The buyer's terms apply as they were the 'last shot' fired before performance
The court will apply a 'reasonable' mix of both parties' terms

bank.question: If there is a conflict between two or more of the SRA Principles 2019, which Principle takes precedence?
bank.explanation: The SRA Principles 2019 state that where there is a conflict between the Principles, the one which best serves the public interest in the administration of justice takes precedence.
options: Upholding the constitutional principle of the rule of law and the proper administration of justice
Acting in the best interests of each client
Acting with integrity
Maintaining public trust and confidence in the solicitors' profession

bank.question: In the law of contract, when is an acceptance by post generally effective?
bank.explanation: The 'postal rule' (Adams v Lindsell) states that an acceptance is effective the moment it is posted, provided it is reasonable to use the post.
options: When the letter is received by the offeror
When the offeror reads the letter
When the letter is delivered to the offeror's address
The moment the letter is posted by the offeree

bank.question: Under the SRA Code of Conduct for Firms, what must a firm report 'promptly' to the SRA?
bank.explanation: Under PAD 2017, a firm must notify the SRA if they have reasonable grounds to believe there has been a serious breach of the regulatory arrangements.
options: Any technical breach of the SRA Accounts Rules
A serious breach of the SRA regulatory arrangements
A client's failure to pay an invoice within 30 days
A dispute between two partners regarding the firm's strategic direction

bank.question: An employee is given pounds200 by their employer specifically to buy office supplies. Instead, the employee uses it to pay a personal debt. Can this be theft?
bank.explanation: Property remains 'belonging to another' if it is received under an obligation to retain and deal with it in a particular way (Theft Act 1968, s 5(3)).
options: No, because ownership of the money passed to the employee
No, because the employee intended to pay it back
Yes, because legal title stayed with the employer under a resulting trust
Yes, because the money was received under an obligation to deal with it in a specific way

bank.question: In a criminal case where the burden of proof shifts to the defendant (e.g., a plea of insanity), what is the standard of proof?
bank.explanation: The standard of proof for the defendant to prove a defence (where the burden shifts) is the balance of probabilities.
options: Beyond reasonable doubt
On the balance of probabilities
To a point where the jury is 'sure'
To the best of their ability

bank.question: Under what circumstances may a police officer enter private premises without a warrant under common law?
bank.explanation: Common law allows the police to enter without a warrant to deal with or prevent a breach of the peace.
options: To prevent or stop a breach of the peace
To search for evidence of a summary offence
To check if a person has a valid TV licence
To verify the immigration status of an occupant

bank.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the 'Overriding Objective' of the Civil Procedure Rules (CPR)?
bank.explanation: The overriding objective is to enable the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost. Increasing court fees is not an element of this objective.
options: Ensuring that the parties are on an equal footing
Saving expense
Dealing with the case in ways which are proportionate to the amount of money involved
Ensuring that court fees are increased annually to support the judiciary

bank.question: Under the Companies Act 2006, what is the minimum number of directors required for a public company (PLC)?
bank.explanation: Under Section 1 of the Companies Act 2006, a public company must have at least two directors. A private company only needs one.
options: One
Four
Two
Three

bank.question: A solicitor receives a cheque for pounds1,000 from a client to cover the estimated cost of Counsel's fees. How should this money be classified under the SRA Accounts Rules?
bank.explanation: Under the SRA Accounts Rules, money for 'out-of-pocket' expenses (disbursements) for which the firm is liable (like Counsel's fees) is categorized as client money.
options: Client money
Office money
Suspense account money
Trust money for the barrister

bank.question: In a personal injury claim, which of the following is usually classified as 'Special Damages'?
bank.explanation: Special damages are those that can be calculated specifically at the time of the trial, such as loss of earnings up to the date of judgement. Pain and suffering fall under 'General Damages'.
options: Pain, suffering, and loss of amenity
Future loss of earnings
Loss of earnings incurred up to the date of the trial
Loss of future earning capacity

bank.question: Which of the following best describes a 'fixed charge' in corporate finance?
bank.explanation: A fixed charge applies to specific, identifiable assets and prevents the company from dealing with those assets without the lender's consent.
options: A charge over all the company's current and future assets
A charge over a specific, identifiable asset which prevents the company from dealing with it
A charge that only becomes active upon the company going into liquidation
A charge that allows the company to sell the asset in the ordinary course of business

bank.question: A solicitor receives a payment of pounds2,000 from a client on account of future legal costs. Into which account must the solicitor pay this money?
bank.explanation: Under the SRA Accounts Rules, money received from a client for anticipated costs and disbursements is 'client money' and must be paid into a client account.
options: The firm's business account
A client account
A designated suspense account
A separate interest-bearing savings account in the firm's name

bank.question: What are the five essential elements of theft under the Theft Act 1968?
bank.explanation: Under Section 1 of the Theft Act 1968, the five elements are: appropriation, property, belonging to another, dishonesty, and intention to permanently deprive.
options: Appropriation, property, belonging to another, dishonesty, and intention to permanently deprive
Taking, carrying away, property, belonging to another, and lack of consent
Appropriation, tangible goods, belonging to another, and dishonesty
Dishonesty, gain for self, loss to another, and intention to permanently deprive

bank.question: Under the Companies Act 2006, what is the primary duty of a director regarding the 'success of the company'?
bank.explanation: Directors have a statutory duty under s172 Companies Act 2006 to act in a way they consider, in good faith, would be most likely to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole.
options: To act in the best interests of the company's creditors at all times
To maximize short-term profits for the shareholders
To promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole
To prioritize the interests of the company's employees over the shareholders

bank.question: Select two answers. In the law of contract, which of the following statements correctly describe the rules regarding the revocation of an offer sent by post?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (The revocation is effective only when received by the offeree), C (The postal rule does not apply to the revocation of an offer). The postal rule applies only to acceptances, not revocations. Revocations must be communicated to be effective.
options: The revocation is effective only when received by the offeree
The revocation is effective as soon as it is posted by the offeror
The postal rule does not apply to the revocation of an offer
A revocation sent by post is effective even if it never arrives

bank.question: Select two answers. Which of the following are established principles of consideration in English contract law?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (Consideration must move from the promisee but need not move to the promisor), D (Performing an existing legal duty is always sufficient consideration for a new promise). Past consideration is generally not good consideration (Re McArdle), and performing an existing public duty is not sufficient unless it exceeds that duty.
options: Past consideration is always valid if the parties intended to pay later
Consideration must move from the promisee but need not move to the promisor
Consideration must be sufficient but need not be adequate
Performing an existing legal duty is always sufficient consideration for a new promise

bank.question: Under the Caparo test for establishing a duty of care in negligence, which three criteria must be satisfied?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (Reasonable foreseeability of harm), B (A relationship of proximity between the parties), D (Whether it is fair, just, and reasonable to impose a duty). Relevant factors for a duty of care in professional negligence include foreseeability, proximity, and whether it is fair, just, and reasonable.
options: Reasonable foreseeability of harm
A relationship of proximity between the parties
The defendant's personal financial wealth
Whether it is fair, just, and reasonable to impose a duty

bank.question: Select two answers. What are the formal requirements for a valid legal mortgage over registered land in England and Wales?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (It must be created by a deed (compliant with s.1 LPMPA 1989)), C (It must be registered at the Land Registry to be a legal interest). A legal mortgage over land must be created by deed and registered at the Land Registry to take effect at law.
options: It can be created by a simple oral agreement
It must be created by a deed (compliant with s.1 LPMPA 1989)
It must be registered at the Land Registry to be a legal interest
It constitutes a transfer of the entire legal fee simple to the lender

bank.question: Select two answers. In relation to the Equality Act 2010, which of the following statements are correct regarding discrimination?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (Direct discrimination occurs when a person is treated less favourably because of a protected characteristic), D (The Equality Act 2010 only applies to internal employees, not job applicants). Direct discrimination occurs when someone is treated less favourably because of a protected characteristic, and it generally cannot be justified (except for age).
options: Direct discrimination occurs when a person is treated less favourably because of a protected characteristic
Direct discrimination can always be justified if it is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim
Indirect discrimination involves a provision, criterion, or practice that puts a group at a disadvantage
The Equality Act 2010 only applies to internal employees, not job applicants

bank.question: Select two answers. Regarding company decision-making under the Companies Act 2006, which of the following are true?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (An ordinary resolution is passed by a simple majority (more than 50%)), C (A special resolution is required to change a company's name). Ordinary resolutions usually require a simple majority (>50%), while special resolutions require at least 75%.
options: An ordinary resolution is passed by a simple majority (more than 50%)
A special resolution is passed by a 90% majority
A special resolution is required to change a company's name
Public companies can pass written resolutions instead of holding meetings

bank.question: Select two answers. Which of the following are elements of the 'actus reus' of theft under the Theft Act 1968?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (Appropriation is an element of the actus reus), C (Property belonging to another is an element of the actus reus). The actus reus of theft requires the appropriation of property belonging to another; the intention to permanently deprive is part of the mens rea.
options: Dishonesty is an element of the actus reus
Appropriation is an element of the actus reus
Property belonging to another is an element of the actus reus
Intention to permanently deprive is an element of the actus reus

bank.question: Select two answers. Which of the following are the three main divisions of the High Court of Justice?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (The Chancery Division), D (The King's Bench Division). The High Court consists of the Queen's Bench (now King's Bench), Chancery, and Family Divisions. The Crown Court is for criminal matters.
options: The Chancery Division
The Crown Court Division
The High Court of Parliament
The King's Bench Division

bank.question: Select two answers. Which statements correctly describe the tort of trespass to land?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (It is actionable per se (without proof of damage)), D (It can only be committed by someone who intended to cause harm). Trespass to land is actionable per se (without proof of damage) and must be a direct, physical interference.
options: It requires proof of actual financial loss
It is actionable per se (without proof of damage)
It must involve a direct and physical interference with land
It can only be committed by someone who intended to cause harm

bank.question: Select two answers. Which of the following can constitute 'overriding interests' that bind a purchaser of registered land?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (Legal leases for 7 years or less), B (Interests of persons in actual occupation (subject to conditions)). Overriding interests, such as those of persons in actual occupation, can bind a purchaser even if not registered on the title.
options: Legal leases for 7 years or less
Interests of persons in actual occupation (subject to conditions)
A restrictive covenant created in 2020
An equitable mortgage not protected by a notice

bank.question: Select two answers. In civil litigation, what are the key differences between the 'Standard Basis' and 'Indemnity Basis' of costs assessment?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are C (Under the Standard Basis, costs must be proportionately incurred), D (Under the Indemnity Basis, there is no requirement for costs to be proportionate). The Standard Basis is the default where the court resolves doubt in favour of the paying party; the Indemnity Basis resolves doubt in favour of the receiving party.
options: Under the Standard Basis, the court resolves doubt in favour of the receiving party
Under the Indemnity Basis, the court resolves doubt in favour of the paying party
Under the Standard Basis, costs must be proportionately incurred
Under the Indemnity Basis, there is no requirement for costs to be proportionate

bank.question: Select two answers. For a claim of unfair dismissal to succeed, which of the following must be established?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (The employer must show a statutory fair reason, such as conduct or capability), C (The dismissal must be procedurally fair under all the circumstances). To be fair, a dismissal must be for a statutory fair reason and the employer must follow a fair procedure. Redundancy is a fair reason.
options: The employer must show a statutory fair reason, such as conduct or capability
An employee needs 5 years of service to claim unfair dismissal
The dismissal must be procedurally fair under all the circumstances
Constructive dismissal never counts as unfair dismissal

bank.question: Under the Accessories and Abettors Act 1861, which two of the following elements are required for a defendant to be liable as an accomplice?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (The accessory must intend to assist or encourage the principal's act), D (The accessory must have knowledge of the essential matters of the principal's offence). For an accessory to be liable, they must intend to assist or encourage the principal and have knowledge of the essential matters of the offence.
options: The accessory must be present at the scene of the crime
The accessory must intend to assist or encourage the principal's act
The accessory must have a motive for the crime to be committed
The accessory must have knowledge of the essential matters of the principal's offence

bank.question: Select two answers. In contract law, what are the three main ways a claimant can establish undue influence to set aside a contract?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (Actual undue influence (pressure)), C (A relationship of trust and confidence combined with a transaction that requires explanation). Undue influence can be established through actual pressure or a relationship of trust where a transaction calls for explanation.
options: Actual undue influence (pressure)
The legal doctrine of 'caveat emptor'
A relationship of trust and confidence combined with a transaction that requires explanation
An imbalance of bargaining power alone

bank.question: Regarding the voting thresholds for shareholder resolutions under the Companies Act 2006, which two of the following are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (An ordinary resolution is passed by a simple majority (more than 50%) of those voting), C (A special resolution requires a majority of not less than 75% of those voting). Unless the articles say otherwise, ordinary resolutions are passed by a simple majority and special resolutions by a 75% majority of those voting.
options: An ordinary resolution requires exactly 51% of the total voting rights of the company
An ordinary resolution is passed by a simple majority (more than 50%) of those voting
A special resolution requires a majority of not less than 75% of those voting
A special resolution requires a unanimous vote of all shareholders

bank.question: According to the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, which two conditions allow a third party to enforce a contract term?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (The contract expressly provides that the third party may enforce the term), C (The term purports to confer a benefit on the third party (and the parties intended it to be enforceable)). Under the doctrine of privity, only those who are party to a contract or qualify under the 1999 Act's specific criteria can enforce its terms.
options: The contract expressly provides that the third party may enforce the term
The third party has provided consideration for the promise
The term purports to confer a benefit on the third party (and the parties intended it to be enforceable)
The third party was present at the signing of the contract

bank.question: Select two answers. Under CPR Part 24, which three of the following conditions might lead a court to grant summary judgment?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (The claimant has no real prospect of succeeding on the claim or issue), D (There is no other compelling reason why the case or issue should be disposed of at a trial). Summary judgment is appropriate when there is no real prospect of success and no other compelling reason for a trial.
options: The claimant has a better than 50% chance of winning at trial
The claimant has no real prospect of succeeding on the claim or issue
The defendant has no real prospect of successfully defending the claim or issue
There is no other compelling reason why the case or issue should be disposed of at a trial

bank.question: In criminal law, which two statements correctly describe the requirements for the defence of self-defence?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (The force used must be reasonable in the circumstances as the defendant believed them to be), D (The defendant must prove their innocence beyond a reasonable doubt). Self-defence requires the force used to be necessary and objectively reasonable based on the facts as the defendant honestly believed them.
options: The force used must be reasonable in the circumstances as the defendant believed them to be
The defendant must have attempted to retreat before using any force
The force used must be proportionate to the threat perceived
The defendant must prove their innocence beyond a reasonable doubt

bank.question: Which three of the following are essential requirements for the doctrine of promissory estoppel to apply?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (There must be a clear and unequivocal promise or representation), B (The representee must have acted in reliance on the promise), C (It must be inequitable for the promisor to go back on the promise). Promissory estoppel prevents a party from going back on a promise that was intended to be binding and was acted upon to the other's detriment.
options: There must be a clear and unequivocal promise or representation
The representee must have acted in reliance on the promise
It must be inequitable for the promisor to go back on the promise
It can be used as a 'sword' to create a new cause of action

bank.question: Select 1 answers. To be a legal easement over registered land, which two of the following requirements must be met?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (A legal easement must be created by deed). Legal easements for a term equivalent to a fee simple or a term of years must be created by deed and registered to be legal.
options: A legal easement can be created orally if it is for less than three years
A legal easement must be created by deed
A legal easement must be for a period of at least 21 years
A legal easement must be registered against the servient title if the land is registered

bank.question: Regarding the SRA Code of Conduct, which two of the following are mandatory obligations for solicitors?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are C (Solicitors must keep client money separate from the firm's money), D (Solicitors must act in a way that upholds public trust and confidence in the profession). Professional conduct rules require solicitors to protect client money and maintain high standards of honesty/integrity.
options: Solicitors may use client money to pay for the firm's office rent temporarily
Solicitors are allowed to accept any gift from a client without disclosure
Solicitors must keep client money separate from the firm's money
Solicitors must act in a way that upholds public trust and confidence in the profession

bank.question: Under the Civil Evidence Act 1995, which two statements correctly describe the treatment of hearsay evidence in civil litigation?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (Hearsay evidence is generally admissible in civil proceedings), C (The weight given to hearsay evidence is at the discretion of the court). Hearsay is generally admissible in civil proceedings but its weight may be challenged, and notice should be given to the other side.
options: Hearsay evidence is strictly prohibited in all civil trials
Hearsay evidence is generally admissible in civil proceedings
The weight given to hearsay evidence is at the discretion of the court
Notice of hearsay evidence must only be given if the witness is deceased

bank.question: Which two of the following are correct regarding the procedure and requirements for Judicial Review?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (The claimant must have a 'sufficient interest' (standing) in the matter), D (Judicial review is an appeal on the facts of the case). Judicial review is the process by which courts supervise the exercise of power by public bodies, not a merits-based appeal.
options: The claimant must have a 'sufficient interest' (standing) in the matter
The court can replace the public body's decision with its own preferred outcome
The claim must generally be filed within three months of the grounds arising
Judicial review is an appeal on the facts of the case

bank.question: Which three elements must be satisfied to establish vicarious liability of an employer for the acts of an employee?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (There must be a relationship of employment or one 'akin to employment'), C (The employee must have committed a tort), D (The tort must have been committed in the 'course of employment'). Vicarious liability requires an employment-like relationship, a tort committed by the employee, and that it occurred in the course of employment.
options: There must be a relationship of employment or one 'akin to employment'
The employer must have been personally negligent in supervising the employee
The employee must have committed a tort
The tort must have been committed in the 'course of employment'

bank.question: Under the Companies Act 2006, which two of the following statements regarding shareholder resolutions and meetings are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (A special resolution requires a majority of not less than 75% of the votes cast), C (The minimum notice period for a general meeting of a private limited company is 14 clear days). Special resolutions require at least 75% of votes cast, and general meetings of private companies usually require 14 days' notice unless short notice is agreed.
options: A special resolution requires a majority of not less than 75% of the votes cast
An ordinary resolution requires a majority of 75% of the votes cast
The minimum notice period for a general meeting of a private limited company is 14 clear days
A written resolution can be used by public limited companies to pass any resolution

bank.question: In criminal law, which two statements correctly describe the nature of strict liability offences?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (Strict liability offences do not require proof of mens rea for at least one element of the actus reus), D (There is a common law presumption that mens rea is required unless Parliament clearly indicates otherwise). Strict liability offences do not require proof of mens rea for at least one part of the actus reus, and there is a common law presumption that Parliament intends mens rea to be required.
options: Strict liability offences require proof of intention for all elements of the crime
Strict liability offences do not require proof of mens rea for at least one element of the actus reus
The prosecution must prove a 'guilty mind' for every element of a strict liability offence
There is a common law presumption that mens rea is required unless Parliament clearly indicates otherwise

bank.question: Which two of the following statements are true regarding the rules of consideration in contract law?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (Consideration must be sufficient but need not be adequate), C (Past consideration is generally not good consideration for a new promise). Consideration must be sufficient (have some value) but need not be adequate (of equal market value), and past consideration is generally not valid consideration.
options: Consideration must be adequate and match the market value of the promise
Consideration must be sufficient but need not be adequate
Past consideration is generally not good consideration for a new promise
Performance of an existing legal duty is always sufficient consideration for a new promise

bank.question: In the law of contract, which two of the following statements regarding specific performance are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (Specific performance is an equitable remedy and is granted at the court's discretion), D (Specific performance is generally not granted if damages would be an adequate remedy). Specific performance is a discretionary equitable remedy, and it is usually refused if damages would be an adequate remedy for the claimant.
options: Specific performance is an equitable remedy and is granted at the court's discretion
Specific performance is a right for any breach of a contract for the sale of goods
The court will grant specific performance even if it requires constant supervision
Specific performance is generally not granted if damages would be an adequate remedy

bank.question: Under the Human Rights Act 1998, which two of the following statements are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (Legislation must be read and given effect in a way which is compatible with Convention rights so far as it is possible to do so), B (It is unlawful for a public authority to act in a way which is incompatible with a Convention right). The Human Rights Act 1998 requires legislation to be interpreted compatibly with Convention rights where possible and makes it unlawful for public authorities to act incompatibly with them.
options: Legislation must be read and given effect in a way which is compatible with Convention rights so far as it is possible to do so
It is unlawful for a public authority to act in a way which is incompatible with a Convention right
Section 3 allows courts to strike down primary legislation that is incompatible with the ECHR
The Act applies to private individuals in the same way it applies to public authorities

bank.question: According to the SRA Standards and Regulations, which two of the following are professional obligations for solicitors?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are C (Solicitors must maintain professional indemnity insurance in accordance with SRA rules), D (Solicitors must act with integrity at all times). Professional indemnity insurance must be maintained at all times, and solicitors must act with integrity as per the SRA Principles.
options: Solicitors are permitted to act where there is a significant risk of a conflict of interest with their own interests
Solicitors should prioritize their own interests over the interests of the client
Solicitors must maintain professional indemnity insurance in accordance with SRA rules
Solicitors must act with integrity at all times

bank.question: Which two statements regarding the burden and standard of proof in civil litigation are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (The standard of proof in civil proceedings is the balance of probabilities), C (The burden of proof generally lies with the claimant). The standard of proof in civil cases is the balance of probabilities, and the burden of proof generally rests with the claimant.
options: The standard of proof in civil proceedings is the balance of probabilities
The standard of proof in civil proceedings is beyond reasonable doubt
The burden of proof generally lies with the claimant
The burden of proof always shifts to the defendant once a claim form is issued

bank.question: In land law, which two of the following statements regarding registered land are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (Legal leases for a term of seven years or less do not need to be registered to be legal), D (Registered land rules for adverse possession are the same as those for unregistered land). Legal leases of 7 years or less do not require registration to bind a purchaser, and adverse possession of registered land is governed by the Land Registration Act 2002.
options: Legal leases for a term of seven years or less do not need to be registered to be legal
Equitable interests must always be registered as a charge to bind a purchaser
A transfer of registered land must be completed by registration to vest the legal estate in the transferee
Registered land rules for adverse possession are the same as those for unregistered land

bank.question: Under the Partnership Act 1890, which two statements correctly describe a partner's authority to bind the firm?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (Every partner is an agent of the firm and their other partners for the purpose of the business), D (The firm is bound by a partner's acts if they are carrying on the business of the firm in the usual way). A partner is an agent of the firm and has 'apparent' or 'ostensible' authority to bind the firm in transactions within the usual scope of the business.
options: A partner has no authority to bind the firm unless express permission is given
Every partner is an agent of the firm and their other partners for the purpose of the business
A partner cannot bind the firm if they have exceeded their internal authority
The firm is bound by a partner's acts if they are carrying on the business of the firm in the usual way

bank.question: In the law of negligence, which two of the following statements are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (Whether a duty of care exists is determined by foreseeability, proximity, and whether it is fair, just, and reasonable), C (The standard of care is an objective test of the reasonable person). A duty of care is established using the Caparo test (foreseeability, proximity, fairness), and the standard of care is that of the reasonably competent person in that role.
options: Whether a duty of care exists is determined by foreseeability, proximity, and whether it is fair, just, and reasonable
The standard of care is a subjective test based on the individual defendant's skill level
The standard of care is an objective test of the reasonable person
Breach of duty is always presumed if an accident occurs

bank.question: Regarding company officers under the Companies Act 2006, which two statements are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (A public limited company must have at least two directors), C (A public limited company must have a qualified company secretary). Public limited companies (PLCs) must have at least two directors and a qualified company secretary.
options: A public limited company must have at least one director
A public limited company must have at least two directors
A public limited company must have a qualified company secretary
A private limited company is required by law to have a company secretary

bank.question: In criminal law, which two statements are correct regarding the offence of Grievous Bodily Harm (GBH)?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (Grievous Bodily Harm (GBH) means 'really serious bodily harm'), B (GBH can include serious psychiatric or psychological injury). Grievous bodily harm (GBH) refers to 'really serious bodily harm' as defined in DPP v Smith, and it can include psychiatric injury.
options: Grievous Bodily Harm (GBH) means 'really serious bodily harm'
GBH can include serious psychiatric or psychological injury
The word 'maliciously' in Section 18 of the OAPA 1861 means the defendant must act with ill-will or spite
Section 20 of the OAPA 1861 is a higher-level offence requiring specific intent to cause GBH

bank.question: Which two of the following are essential requirements for a successful claim in the tort of private nuisance?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (The claimant must have a proprietary interest in the land affected), C (The interference with the use or enjoyment of land must be substantial and unreasonable). Private nuisance requires the claimant to have a proprietary interest in the land and the interference must be unreasonable rather than just temporary or trivial.
options: The claimant must have a proprietary interest in the land affected
The defendant must have acted with malice in every case to be held liable
The interference with the use or enjoyment of land must be substantial and unreasonable
An action can be brought by anyone who is a guest or visitor at the property at the time of the nuisance

bank.question: Select two answers. Under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, which three conditions must be met for a duty of care to arise towards a trespasser?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (The occupier must be aware of the danger or have reasonable grounds to believe it exists), D (The occupier must know or have reasonable grounds to believe the trespasser is in the vicinity of the danger). Under s.1(1) of the 1977 Act, the duty is owed by an occupier to persons other than visitors for risks of injury due to the state of the premises.
options: The duty covers damage to personal property brought onto the land by the trespasser
The occupier must be aware of the danger or have reasonable grounds to believe it exists
Occupiers cannot exclude liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence
The occupier must know or have reasonable grounds to believe the trespasser is in the vicinity of the danger

bank.question: Which three of the following statements regarding a company's Articles of Association are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (The articles of association form a statutory contract between the company and its members), B (Amendments to the articles generally require a special resolution of the shareholders), D (The articles are a public document filed with the Registrar of Companies). The Articles are a public contract, are subject to the Companies Act, and bind both the company and its members. A special resolution (75%) is required for changes.
options: The articles of association form a statutory contract between the company and its members
Amendments to the articles generally require a special resolution of the shareholders
A simple majority of 50.1% is sufficient to change any provision in the articles
The articles are a public document filed with the Registrar of Companies

bank.question: Regarding the remedy of specific performance in contract law, which two statements are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (It is a discretionary remedy granted by the court), D (It will generally not be granted for contracts involving personal services). Specific performance is a discretionary equitable remedy and is generally not available for contracts of personal service, such as employment.
options: It is a discretionary remedy granted by the court
It is available as a matter of right whenever a contract is breached
It is commonly used for the sale of generic goods available on the open market
It will generally not be granted for contracts involving personal services

bank.question: Select two answers. Under CPR Part 36, which three of the following are formal requirements for a valid claimant's offer?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (The offer must be made in writing), C (The offer must state on its face that it is intended to have the consequences of Part 36). Part 36 offers must be in writing, state they are intended to have Part 36 consequences, and specify a relevant period of not less than 21 days.
options: The offer can be made orally if witnesses are present
The offer must be made in writing
The offer must state on its face that it is intended to have the consequences of Part 36
The offer must specify a period of at least 21 days within which the defendant will be liable for the claimant's costs if accepted

bank.question: Under the Wills Act 1837 and case law, which two statements regarding testamentary capacity are correct?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are B (The testator must be at least 18 years of age), D (The testator must have a solicitor present for the will to be legally valid). A person must be at least 18 and of sound mind to make a valid will; the 'test' for capacity is found in Banks v Goodfellow.
options: The testator must be at least 21 years of age
The testator must be at least 18 years of age
The testator must understand the nature and effect of making a will
The testator must have a solicitor present for the will to be legally valid

bank.question: According to the SRA Code of Conduct and Principles, which two of the following are mandatory requirements for solicitors?
bank.explanation: The correct answers are A (Solicitors must ensure they have professional indemnity insurance in place), B (Solicitors must act with integrity in all professional dealings). Professional indemnity insurance is a mandatory requirement to protect clients, and solicitors must act with integrity as per SRA Principles.
